topic: Growth, Development, Developmental Stages and the Child as an Individual
subtopic: SAQ 1.1
stem: Distinguish among growth, development, and maturation, and state four reasons why nurses must understand typical child growth and development.
options: Growth is a quantitative physical increase in body size (height, weight, organ size) via cell division and protein synthesis; development is the qualitative, behavioural progression in skills and functional capacity; maturation is a qualitative change produced by the passage of time rather than learning. Nurses need this knowledge to: (1) plan holistic individualized care, (2) anticipate age-expected behaviours, (3) understand caregiver behaviours and age-specific illnesses, and (4) educate mothers to monitor milestones and promote optimal growth.

Prenatal phases: Germinal/pre-embryonic (conception–week 2/3, zygote implantation), Embryonic (weeks 3–8, organogenesis, high teratogen vulnerability), and Fetal (week 9–birth, rapid organ maturation and growth to ~50 cm/3.3 kg). Milestones: 6 months (transfers objects, sits with support, rolls prone-to-supine, palmar grasp, 'mumum'/'dada', stranger shyness); 1 year (stands holding furniture, 2–3 repeated words, waves goodbye, understands simple commands); 3 years (stairs 1 foot/step up, copies circle, 9-cube tower, asks constant questions in sentences, cooperative play).

The Principle of Direction of Growth states growth follows predictable gradients: cephalocaudal (head-to-toe, e.g., brain achieves 70% growth by age 2), proximodistal (midline-to-extremities, gross to fine motor), and symmetric (equal bilateral growth). The Principle of Discontinuity of Growth Rate states that growth alternates between accelerated periods (birth to 2 years and adolescent growth spurt around age 10) and decelerated periods (childhood).

Every child combines unique genetics, life experiences, and environmental interactions. Individuality is modified by family type, ethnic/racial background, religion and social status, diet, living patterns, and relationship attitudes. Understanding individuality enables nurses to provide quality care, help the child attain/maintain/regain optimal health, deliver appropriate stimulation and intervention, and counsel and inform parents effectively.

topic: Developmental Theories of Childhood
subtopic: SAQ 2.1
stem: Define schemas, assimilation, accommodation, and equilibration in Piaget's theory, and list the four stages of cognitive development with their approximate ages.
options: Level 1 Pre-conventional: (1) Obedience & Punishment, (2) Self-Interest/Reward. Level 2 Conventional: (3) Good Interpersonal Relationships/Approval, (4) Law & Order. Level 3 Post-conventional: (5) Social Contract, (6) Universal Ethical Principles. Clinically, nurses explain safety rules simply to young children, discuss fairness and empathy with older children via stories/dilemmas, avoid judging solely by age, and model ethical conduct.

Schemas are organized mental/physical frameworks for interpreting experience; assimilation fits new info into existing schemas; accommodation modifies existing schemas or creates new ones; equilibration balances assimilation and accommodation to advance thinking. The four stages are Sensorimotor (birth–2 yrs), Preoperational (2–7 yrs), Concrete Operational (7–11 yrs), and Formal Operational (11/12 yrs onward).

Stage 0 Primal/Undifferentiated (0–2 yrs, basic trust/safety); Stage 1 Intuitive–Projective (2–7 yrs, stories/imagination); Stage 2 Mythic–Literal (7–12 yrs, literal stories/fairness); Stage 3 Synthetic–Conventional (12+ yrs, conformity to peer/religious authority). Ethical safeguards: never assume religiosity, never impose beliefs/proselytize, balance safe rituals with clinical consent/safety, and never imply illness is punishment or lack of faith.

Ego identity is the conscious sense of self continually developed through social interaction. Erikson's four organizing concepts are stages of development, developmental tasks/goals, psychosocial crisis, and coping process. Preschoolers (3–6 yrs): Initiative vs. Guilt, virtue Purpose, often equate illness with being bad/punishment. Adolescents (12–18 yrs): Identity vs. Role Confusion, virtue Fidelity, commonly react with anger over illness-imposed dependency.

subtopic: In-Text Self-Check
stem: How can childhood tics be clinically differentiated from dystonias and dyskinetic movements?
options: Children under 2 years are measured lying flat (recumbent length) on a length board with two people assisting, whereas children 2 years and older are measured standing barefoot (height) against a vertical stadiometer.

Weight-for-Length/Height below -2 SD indicates Wasting (acute/recent weight loss; below -3 SD is severe), whereas Length/Height-for-Age below -2 SD indicates Stunting (chronic/long-term undernutrition).

Tics are absent during sleep, whereas dystonias and dyskinetic movements are not characterized by complete absence in sleep; additionally, tics are sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic, and worsen under parental pressure.

Symptoms (inattention, motor overactivity, impulsiveness) must be evident before age 7 years, persist for more than 6 months, occur in both home and school settings, and impede the child's functioning.

stem: Describe the assessment and fluid management principles for mild, moderate, and severe dehydration, and list four true contraindications to ORT.
options: The cold chain is an unbroken network of refrigeration and transport from vaccine manufacture to injection protecting vaccines from heat (>8–9°C) and direct sunlight, monitored with colorimetric heat-indicator disks. True contraindications: (1) severe allergic reaction (urticaria, shock, airway obstruction), (2) severe immunosuppression (avoid live BCG/measles/OPV; delay 3 months post-therapy; no BCG in symptomatic AIDS), and (3) previous severe reactions (for pertussis: seizure within 3 days, persistent/high-pitched crying or collapse/shock within 2 days, fever >40.5°C, or anaphylaxis).

EBF gives only breast milk for the first 6 months (no water/solids except ORS, vitamins, minerals, or medicines). Proper latch: mother upright/relaxed, baby's head and body aligned facing mother, mouth opposite nipple, offering whole breast without pinching areola, slow deep sucks without pain. Diet: avoid high-mercury fish, avoid alcohol (impairs infant motor development), limit caffeine to ≤300 mg/day. WHO HIV guideline: use replacement feeding only if acceptable, feasible, affordable, and safe; otherwise exclusively breastfeed for 6 months (introducing solids thereafter while continuing breastfeeding) with maternal/infant ARVs to cut transmission.

1st (Birth): BCG 0.05 mL ID (right upper arm) + OPV0 2 drops oral. 2nd (6 wks): Pentavalent 1 (DPT, HBV, Hib) 0.5 mL IM (anterolateral thigh) + OPV1 2 drops oral. 3rd (10 wks): Pentavalent 2 0.5 mL IM (anterolateral thigh) + OPV2 2 drops oral. 4th (14 wks): Pentavalent 3 0.5 mL IM (anterolateral thigh) + OPV3 2 drops oral. 5th (9 mos): Measles 0.5 mL SC (left upper arm) + Yellow Fever 0.5 mL SC (left upper arm).

Contraindications to ORT: protracted vomiting despite small frequent sips, worsening diarrhoea exceeding intake, stupor/coma, intestinal ileus (and hemodynamic shock with impaired airway reflexes).

options: Homemade ORS mixes 1 litre clean/boiled water with 2.5 mL (1/2 level teaspoon) salt and 30 mL (6 level teaspoons) sugar; discard after 12 hours at room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated. stem: Define female education, explain how maternal education improves child survival, and list five ways to promote women's education in Nigeria.
options: Female education is training females morally and intellectually through formal schooling. Educated mothers have higher child survival via exclusive breastfeeding, better nutrition, prenatal care, higher immunization uptake, and planned family sizes. Five promotion measures: orienting parents and religious/community leaders, prohibiting female child labour/street hawking, discouraging teenage marriage/pregnancy, removing cultural and curricular gender biases, and employing more female teachers in rural areas as mentors.

WHO defines sanitation as providing facilities and services for safe disposal of human urine and faeces. On-site sanitation collects and treats waste where deposited (pit latrines, septic tanks), whereas ecological sanitation hygienically recycles nutrients and water from human/animal waste. Poor sanitation drives up to 5 million annual waterborne deaths—including 1.6–2.5 million diarrhoeal deaths/year (causing ~50% of underweight children), schistosomiasis, trachoma, faecal-oral diseases, and hookworm.

stem: Name the four main human Plasmodium species, identify which is deadliest, and list six major signs/symptoms and four severe complications of malaria.
options: First-line ACTs: artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem), artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, and artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. Five prevention strategies: universal Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs), Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS), Intermittent Preventive Treatment with SP in pregnancy (IPTp) and infants (IPTi), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC in Sahel under-5s), and eliminating stagnant mosquito breeding water plus WHO T3 (Test, Treat, Track) surveillance.

Species: Plasmodium falciparum (deadliest), P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale (plus zoonotic P. knowlesi). Signs/symptoms: fever, shivering, joint pain (arthralgia), vomiting, haemolytic anaemia, jaundice, haemoglobinuria, convulsions, retinal damage, abnormal posturing. topic: Childhood Communicable Diseases II: Tetanus and Pneumonia
subtopic: SAQ 7.1
stem: List the four clinical classifications of tetanus and state any six points of entry for Clostridium tetani.
options: Stages: (1) Congestion—dilated capillary permeability leaks serous exudate, fibrinogen, plasma proteins, and RBCs into alveoli; (2) Red Hepatization—hyperaemia and organism proliferation in alveolar fluid; (3) Gray Hepatization/Consolidation—thick exudates fill alveoli making gas exchange impossible (causing dyspnoea), plus reduced surfactant leading to atelectasis. Six complications: shock, atelectasis, pleural effusion, pleuritis, lung abscess, and respiratory failure (ARDS).

Directed cough: assume proper position, perform deep inspiration, close glottis, contract expiratory muscles against closed glottis, suddenly open glottis, and produce explosive expiration. Prevention: avoid indiscriminate antibiotics in minor viral URIs, administer pneumococcal (PCV13/pneumovax) and influenza vaccines, turn unconscious/bedridden patients frequently with deep-breathing/early ambulation, elevate head during and ≥30 min after NG tube feeds (prefer oral tube), discourage force-feeding children, and practise proper cough hygiene/secretion disposal.

Classifications: Generalised tetanus (~80%, descending lockjaw/risus sardonicus/opisthotonus), Neonatal tetanus (non-sterile umbilical cord cutting), Local tetanus (localized spasm near wound), and Cephalic tetanus (cranial/facial nerve involvement from ear/head infection). Six points of entry: post-traumatic wounds, deep penetrating dirty wounds, burns, umbilical cord stump, post-puerperal/abortal contaminated instruments, and crush/dead-tissue injuries (also post-surgical, chronic ulcers/otitis media, healed wounds).

options: Microbiological: viral, bacterial (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, Klebsiella, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Mycobacterium, Rickettsia), hypostatic, protozoal (Pneumocystis carinii), and fungal. Anatomical: bronchopneumonia (diffuse distal airways/alveoli, common in children), lobar/lobular (part/whole lobe, common in adults), and interstitial. CAP begins in the community or within the first 2 days of admission (often S. pneumoniae; ATS Categories 1–4), whereas HAP occurs ≥48 hours after admission in a non-incubating patient (often Pseudomonas, Enterobacter, S. aureus; early <5 days vs. late >5 days).

Classifications: Generalised tetanus (~80%, descending lockjaw/risus sardonicus/opisthotonus), Neonatal tetanus (non-sterile umbilical cord cutting), Local tetanus (localized spasm near wound), and Cephalic tetanus (cranial/facial nerve involvement from ear/head infection). Six points of entry: post-traumatic wounds, deep penetrating dirty wounds, burns, umbilical cord stump, post-puerperal/abortal contaminated instruments, and crush/dead-tissue injuries (also post-surgical, chronic ulcers/otitis media, healed wounds).

Directed cough: assume proper position, perform deep inspiration, close glottis, contract expiratory muscles against closed glottis, suddenly open glottis, and produce explosive expiration. Prevention: avoid indiscriminate antibiotics in minor viral URIs, administer pneumococcal (PCV13/pneumovax) and influenza vaccines, turn unconscious/bedridden patients frequently with deep-breathing/early ambulation, elevate head during and ≥30 min after NG tube feeds (prefer oral tube), discourage force-feeding children, and practise proper cough hygiene/secretion disposal.

Chemotherapy: debride wound with H2O2, administer metronidazole (drug of choice) or high-dose crystalline penicillin to stop toxin production, neutralize unbound toxin with TIG or ATS (20,000 IU IM), and control spasms/ANS instability with alternating diazepam and chlorpromazine (or morphine/phenobarbitone). Nursing care: isolate in a quiet dark room ('No-Noise' sign), admit on padded fracture bed, perform care at peak sedation, handle gently, keep suction/O2/tracheotomy ready, maintain IV/NG fluids and nutrition, open a spasm chart, provide wound H2O2/oxygen care, and initiate physiotherapy during recovery.

stem: Explain the meaning of hospitalization to a preschooler and an adolescent, and describe the three common behavioural reactions of children to hospitalization.
options: Diarrhoea plans: Plan A (no dehydration—home extra fluids and continued feeding), Plan B (some dehydration—ORS in clinic over 4 hours), Plan C (severe dehydration—IV fluids or urgent referral), always adding zinc for 10–14 days. stem: Complete this statement about Family Planning and Classification of Contraceptive Methods: Contraceptives fall into five main groups: (1) Barrier Methods—Condoms (latex male/female sheaths preventing sperm entry, requiring no prescription, and uniquely protecting against STDs), Diaphragm and Cervical Cap (provider-fitted rubber cup with spermicide over the cervix, left 6+ hours post-coitus; risks include irritation, UTI, rare toxic shock syndrome if left too long, or abnormal Pap with cap), and Vaginal Sponge (moistened spermicide-saturated synthetic sponge); (2) Hormonal Methods—using oestrogen plus progestin or progestin alone to inhibit ovulation and thicken cervical mucus: combined pills, progestin-only mini-pills, subdermal implants, 3-monthly progestin injections (Depo-Provera), skin patches (Ortho Evra), vaginal rings (NuvaRing), and emergency ('morning after') contraception; (3) Intrauterine Device (IUD)—provider-inserted plastic/copper or progestin-releasing uterine device lasting 5–10+ years with <1% annual failure (risks: cramps, heavy bleeding, uterine perforation; progestin IUD may cause ____ on removal); (4) Permanent Methods—Tubal Ligation (severing/blocking fallopian tubes) and Vasectomy (blocking vas deferens); and (5) Unreliable / Natural Methods—Coitus Interruptus (withdrawal; pre-ejaculatory semen risks pregnancy), Post-coital Douching (ineffective as sperm pass the cervix within seconds), Fertility Awareness (charting basal temperature, cervical mucus, or calendar), Breastfeeding (lactation alone does not guarantee infertility), and Complete Abstinence (the only 100% effective method against pregnancy and STDs, though difficult to sustain).

explanation.correct: Family Planning and Classification of Contraceptive Methods: Contraceptives fall into five main groups: (1) Barrier Methods—Condoms (latex male/female sheaths preventing sperm entry, requiring no prescription, and uniquely protecting against STDs), Diaphragm and Cervical Cap (provider-fitted rubber cup with spermicide over the cervix, left 6+ hours post-coitus; risks include irritation, UTI, rare toxic shock syndrome if left too long, or abnormal Pap with cap), and Vaginal Sponge (moistened spermicide-saturated synthetic sponge); (2) Hormonal Methods—using oestrogen plus progestin or progestin alone to inhibit ovulation and thicken cervical mucus: combined pills, progestin-only mini-pills, subdermal implants, 3-monthly progestin injections (Depo-Provera), skin patches (Ortho Evra), vaginal rings (NuvaRing), and emergency ('morning after') contraception; (3) Intrauterine Device (IUD)—provider-inserted plastic/copper or progestin-releasing uterine device lasting 5–10+ years with <1% annual failure (risks: cramps, heavy bleeding, uterine perforation; progestin IUD may cause spotting then amenorrhoea reversible on removal); (4) Permanent Methods—Tubal Ligation (severing/blocking fallopian tubes) and Vasectomy (blocking vas deferens); and (5) Unreliable / Natural Methods—Coitus Interruptus (withdrawal; pre-ejaculatory semen risks pregnancy), Post-coital Douching (ineffective as sperm pass the cervix within seconds), Fertility Awareness (charting basal temperature, cervical mucus, or calendar), Breastfeeding (lactation alone does not guarantee infertility), and Complete Abstinence (the only 100% effective method against pregnancy and STDs, though difficult to sustain).

topic: Principles of Care for the Hospitalized Child and Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI / IMCI)
subtopic: Six-Step IMNCI Case Management Process, Danger Signs, and Main Symptom Classifications
stem: Complete this statement about Six-Step IMNCI Case Management Process, Danger Signs, and Main Symptom Classifications: Next assess four Main Symptoms: (a) Cough/Difficult Breathing (count breaths for 1 full minute; fast breathing cut-offs: ≥50/min for 2–12 months, ≥40/min for 12 months–5 years; check chest indrawing and calm stridor)—Pink (danger sign or calm stridor -> urgent referral), Yellow (fast breathing or chest indrawing -> Pneumonia: oral amoxicillin + follow-up), Green (no pneumonia signs -> soothe throat, home care); (b) Diarrhoea (ask duration/blood; check lethargy, sunken eyes, drinking eagerly/poorly, skin pinch)—Severe dehydration (Plan C: IV fluids/urgent referral), Some dehydration (Plan B: ORS in clinic over 4 hours), No dehydration (Plan A: extra fluids/feeding at home), ALWAYS adding zinc for 10–14 days and continued feeding; (c) Fever (duration, stiff neck, rash, malaria test)—Very severe febrile disease (danger sign/stiff neck -> urgent referral), Malaria (positive test -> national antimalarial/ACT), Measles (rash + cough/runny nose/red eyes -> Vitamin A), Fever no malaria (home care); and (d) Ear Problem (pain, pus duration, tender mastoid swelling)—Mastoiditis (tender behind-ear swelling -> urgent referral), Acute ear infection (pus <14 days or pain -> antibiotic + dry wick), Chronic ear infection (pus ≥14 days -> dry wick + ____).

explanation.correct: Six-Step IMNCI Case Management Process, Danger Signs, and Main Symptom Classifications: Next assess four Main Symptoms: (a) Cough/Difficult Breathing (count breaths for 1 full minute; fast breathing cut-offs: ≥50/min for 2–12 months, ≥40/min for 12 months–5 years; check chest indrawing and calm stridor)—Pink (danger sign or calm stridor -> urgent referral), Yellow (fast breathing or chest indrawing -> Pneumonia: oral amoxicillin + follow-up), Green (no pneumonia signs -> soothe throat, home care); (b) Diarrhoea (ask duration/blood; check lethargy, sunken eyes, drinking eagerly/poorly, skin pinch)—Severe dehydration (Plan C: IV fluids/urgent referral), Some dehydration (Plan B: ORS in clinic over 4 hours), No dehydration (Plan A: extra fluids/feeding at home), ALWAYS adding zinc for 10–14 days and continued feeding; (c) Fever (duration, stiff neck, rash, malaria test)—Very severe febrile disease (danger sign/stiff neck -> urgent referral), Malaria (positive test -> national antimalarial/ACT), Measles (rash + cough/runny nose/red eyes -> Vitamin A), Fever no malaria (home care); and (d) Ear Problem (pain, pus duration, tender mastoid swelling)—Mastoiditis (tender behind-ear swelling -> urgent referral), Acute ear infection (pus <14 days or pain -> antibiotic + dry wick), Chronic ear infection (pus ≥14 days -> dry wick + topical quinolone drops).

topic: Principles of Care for the Hospitalized Child and Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI / IMCI)
subtopic: Nursing Care Principles, Coping Strategies, and Therapeutic Play for the Hospitalized Child
stem: Complete this statement about Nursing Care Principles, Coping Strategies, and Therapeutic Play for the Hospitalized Child: Pediatric hospital nursing centres on three protective principles: (1) Preventing/Minimizing Separation—top priority for children <5 years by welcoming continuous parental presence, supporting anxious children physically, ____ parents if detachment occurs, coaching parents on leaving/returning, encouraging frequent visits, and leaving a comforting home item; (2) Minimizing Loss of Control—promoting movement during procedures (on a parent's lap or via wheelchairs/mobile beds), time structuring (co-designing a written daily schedule integrating treatments, schoolwork, and play), encouraging age-appropriate self-care and food/bedtime choices, and anticipatory education on child rights; and (3) Preventing/Minimizing Fear of Bodily Injury—pre-procedure preparation, modified atraumatic techniques, repeated explanations against mutilation fears, and pain reduction.

explanation.correct: Nursing Care Principles, Coping Strategies, and Therapeutic Play for the Hospitalized Child: Pediatric hospital nursing centres on three protective principles: (1) Preventing/Minimizing Separation—top priority for children <5 years by welcoming continuous parental presence, supporting anxious children physically, talking frequently about absent parents if detachment occurs, coaching parents on leaving/returning, encouraging frequent visits, and leaving a comforting home item; (2) Minimizing Loss of Control—promoting movement during procedures (on a parent's lap or via wheelchairs/mobile beds), time structuring (co-designing a written daily schedule integrating treatments, schoolwork, and play), encouraging age-appropriate self-care and food/bedtime choices, and anticipatory education on child rights; and (3) Preventing/Minimizing Fear of Bodily Injury—pre-procedure preparation, modified atraumatic techniques, repeated explanations against mutilation fears, and pain reduction.

topic: Principles of Care for the Hospitalized Child and Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI / IMCI)
subtopic: Hospitalization: Age-Specific Perceptions, Preparation, and Common Reactions
stem: Complete this statement about Hospitalization: Age-Specific Perceptions, Preparation, and Common Reactions: Illness and hospitalization carry distinct meanings by developmental stage: (1) Infant—global ____ routines/surroundings and separation from the primary love object; (2) Toddler—highest separation anxiety and fear of desertion, relating illness to concrete circumstances; (3) Preschooler—intense fear of bodily harm, mutilation, castration, and intrusive procedures (strong though slightly less separation anxiety than toddlers), often viewing illness as punishment for wrongdoing; (4) School-Age—fears the physical nature of illness and separation from peers/school status, perceiving an external cause located in the body; and (5) Adolescent—anxious about loss of independence, control, identity, and privacy, able to explain illness as organ/process malfunction.

explanation.correct: Hospitalization: Age-Specific Perceptions, Preparation, and Common Reactions: Illness and hospitalization carry distinct meanings by developmental stage: (1) Infant—global reaction to disrupted familiar routines/surroundings and separation from the primary love object; (2) Toddler—highest separation anxiety and fear of desertion, relating illness to concrete circumstances; (3) Preschooler—intense fear of bodily harm, mutilation, castration, and intrusive procedures (strong though slightly less separation anxiety than toddlers), often viewing illness as punishment for wrongdoing; (4) School-Age—fears the physical nature of illness and separation from peers/school status, perceiving an external cause located in the body; and (5) Adolescent—anxious about loss of independence, control, identity, and privacy, able to explain illness as organ/process malfunction.
